extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and parties in Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB) proceedings; trademark litigators and their counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules governing discovery, disclosures, supplementation, filing, objections, and remedies in inter partes TTAB trademark proceedings under the TBMP and applicable Federal Rules/Trademarks Rules. Focuses on duties of candor, search, supplementation, conferral before motions, limits on filing discovery materials, and sanctions/remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature certification under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(g)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: By signing, an attorney or party certifies that to the best of the person's knowledge, information, and belief formed after a reasonable inquiry: (A) with respect to a disclosure, it is complete and correct as of the time it is made; and (B) with respect to a discovery request, response, or objection, it is: (i) consistent with these rules and warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law, or for establishing new law; (ii) not interposed for any improper purpose, such as to harass, cause unnecessary delay, or needlessly increase the cost of litigation; and (iii) neither unreasonable nor unduly burdensome or expensive, considering the needs of the case, prior discovery in the case, the amount in controversy, and the importance of the issues at stake in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signature constitutes a certification and may subject the signer to sanctions if made in violation of the rule. The certification duty requires making a reasonable inquiry into the factual basis of the response, request or objection. Distinguish this certification from other signature requirements (e.g., Fed. R. Civ. P. 33). A party ordinarily cannot argue a discovery request is proper when propounded by itself but improper when propounded by an adversary, absent persuasive reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to cooperate before filing a motion to compel
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to compel initial disclosures, expert testimony disclosures, or discovery must be supported by a written statement that the moving party or its attorney has made a good faith effort, by conference or correspondence, to resolve the issues with the other party but was unable to do so (37 CFR § 2.120(e)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to filing a motion to compel the moving party must make a good faith effort to resolve the dispute; the Board may require conference with the Board attorney to ensure sufficient effort. Failure to demonstrate a good faith effort can be a basis to deny relief. A written statement supporting the motion must show the good faith effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to thoroughly search records for responsive information
rubrics_metrics.description: A party served with a discovery request has a duty to thoroughly search its records for all information properly sought and to provide such information within the time allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper written response to document requests must state whether responsive documents exist and whether they will be produced or withheld on privilege, state objections with reasons, or state that no responsive documents exist. For ESI, if no form is specified or the party objects, response must state the form intended. Avoid 'dumping' large quantities of unrequested material along with requested items. Failure to search completely may preclude reliance at trial on omitted information unless timely supplemented; estoppel sanctions may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to supplement disclosures and discovery responses (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party who made a disclosure or responded to interrogatories/production/admissions must supplement or correct its disclosure or response in a timely manner if it learns the disclosure/response is incomplete or incorrect in some material respect, unless the additional information has otherwise been made known to the other parties; supplementation for experts extends to information in the report and deposition (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(e)(1)-(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplement promptly when new material information is learned; prompt supplementation while discovery remains open generally avoids exclusion of testimony or information. Holding back material items to disclose at the last minute may lead to preclusion under Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(c)(1). However, if information has otherwise been made known during discovery (e.g., deposition), supplementation may not be required. The Board may also order supplementation by its own directive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of untimely or incomplete disclosures (preclusion and sanctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party who provides an incomplete response due to an inadequate records search may not later rely at trial on information properly sought but not included, unless the response is timely supplemented; failure to supplement timely can lead to preclusion under Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(c)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board policy: if omissions are promptly cured (initiative of disclosing party or after notification) while discovery remains open, neither the expert testimony nor omitted information will be excluded. The Board also recognizes circumstances where ESI lost through routine, good-faith operation of systems is not sanctionable. Note: subsections (A) and (B) of Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(c)(1) do not apply in Board proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on filing discovery materials with the Board
rubrics_metrics.description: Written disclosures, documents, discovery depositions, answers to interrogatories, admissions, and other discovery materials should not be filed with the Board except when: (1) submitted with a motion relating to discovery; (2) in support of or response to a motion for summary judgment; (3) under a notice of reliance during a party's testimony period to the extent permitted; or (4) as exhibits to a testimony deposition (37 CFR § 2.120(j)(8)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not routinely file initial or expert disclosures with the Board; instead file a notice that such disclosure was made when necessary. When objecting to proffered evidence or moving to strike testimony on grounds related to discovery/disclosures, submit the pertinent requests/responses/disclosures in support. Specific categories permissible under notice of reliance are limited (adverse party's discovery deposition, answer to interrogatory, admission; printed publications; official records).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification to the Board of expert disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: While copies of expert documents should not be filed with the Board, a party that has disclosed plans to use an expert should file a notice that it has made the required disclosure (Misc. Changes, 72 Fed. Reg. 42242).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notifying the Board can permit suspension of proceedings to allow expert-limited discovery and facilitate discovery planning. Case law indicates notification may not be mandatory if expert-related discovery can be concluded by close of discovery; the Board has discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections to discovery — merits versus attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections challenging the merits of a discovery request include that it is overly broad, unduly vague or ambiguous, burdensome and oppressive, seeks non-discoverable information on expert witnesses, or is not calculated to lead to discovery of admissible evidence. Objections based on confidentiality, privilege, or work product go to attributes of the responsive information, not the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond during the allowed time without excusable neglect may result in forfeiture of the right to object to the merits of the requests. Confidentiality/privilege objections are generally preserved due to the Board's standard protective order; the Board typically will not find those waived simply because other objections are waived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to serve initial disclosures as a ground for objection
rubrics_metrics.description: For proceedings commenced on or after November 1, 2007, failure to serve initial disclosures constitutes a proper ground for objecting to discovery requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party believes it need not respond because the propounding party has not served initial disclosures, the party has a duty to object on that basis rather than simply decline to respond. Case law shows mistaken belief is not a substitute for substantive response or timely objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate method to challenge discovery requests
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally inappropriate to respond to a discovery request by filing a motion attacking it (motion to strike, suppress, or for protective order). Ordinarily a party should respond with information it believes proper and state objections to portions it believes improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions exist where requests constitute clear harassment (e.g., unreasonable number of requests) or where the receiving party was not the real party in interest at commencement; in such cases a motion for protective order or other attack may be proper. For deposition notices that are insufficient, vague, exceed permitted depositions, or are outside the discovery period, motions to quash or for protective order may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and remedy for excessive interrogatories
rubrics_metrics.description: If a responding party believes the number of interrogatories exceeds the limit in 37 CFR § 2.120(d)(1), the responding party must, within the time for serving answers and instead of serving answers and specific objections, serve a general objection on the ground of excessive number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion for a protective order is not the proper method for raising the objection of excessive number. See TBMP § 405.03(e) for remedy guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to compel: timing and prerequisite for sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to compel initial disclosures or expert testimony disclosures must be filed prior to the close of discovery. A motion to compel is a prerequisite to filing a motion for sanctions for failure to make required initial or expert disclosures (37 CFR § 2.120(e); Misc. Changes 72 Fed. Reg. 42242).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board decisions have denied motions for sanctions as premature where no Board order compelling discovery exists. File and pursue a motion to compel first; only after relief is granted may sanctions be sought in many circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for failure to answer interrogatories or produce documents
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party fails to answer an interrogatory or to produce documents, the party seeking discovery may file a motion to compel an answer or production (37 CFR § 2.120(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The seeking party may not immediately obtain sanctions for no response unless the responding party has expressly informed the inquiring party that no response will be made. See TBMP § 523 for motion practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of failure to timely respond to requests for admission
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party fails to file a timely response to requests for admission, the requests will stand admitted unless the party shows failure was due to excusable neglect or a motion to withdraw or amend the admissions under Fed. R. Civ. P. 36(b) is filed and granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If dissatisfied with the sufficiency of an answer/objection, the propounding party may move to determine sufficiency. If Board determines a response does not comply with FRCP 36(a), it may order the matter admitted or require an amended answer; if an objection is unjustified the Board will order a response. Admissions or denials that comply remain proper responses even if they include objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of discovery materials during testimony and by notice of reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (j) will not be interpreted to preclude reading or use of written disclosures or documents, a discovery deposition, or answer to an interrogatory, or admission as part of the examination or cross-examination of any witness during the testimony period (37 CFR § 2.120(j)(6)). Discovery materials should not be filed with the Board except when allowed (see filing limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categories of material that may be submitted by notice of reliance are limited; documents produced in response to document production requests generally cannot be made of record by notice of reliance. Where discovery responses are to be considered on summary judgment, they must be submitted with the motion or responsive brief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board's approach to supplementation of expert disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A party's duty to supplement extends to information included in an expert's report and to information given during the expert's deposition; additions/changes must be disclosed by the time pretrial disclosures are due (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(e)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If deficiencies in expert disclosures are promptly cured once brought to the party's attention, the Board may deny exclusionary relief. The Board may suspend proceedings to allow expert-limited discovery where notice of expert disclosure is given. Case law balances prejudice, opportunity for cross-examination, and timeliness when deciding whether to exclude expert testimony.
